newsitem.title: UK: Ex-Iraq oil minister blames both sides in oil delay.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Iraq oil minister blames both sides in oil delay.

text.p: The man who was the oil minister of Iraq when it invaded Kuwait in 1990 on Monday blamed both Baghdad and Washington for delaying Iraqi oil exports.

Issam al-Chalabi, now a consultant in Amman, Jordan, told an oil conference that he did not believe a United Nations plan to allow Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months would be implemented before the end of 1996.
"I blame both parties, but unfortunately the Iraqi nation is suffering under the sanctions and nobody seems to care, neither the U.S., the U.N. or the Iraqi government," he said.
Chalabi said the United States was employing "delaying tactics" to hamper the deal but he said he "sometimes" would "wonder" if Baghdad wanted the deal to go ahead anyway.
He recalled that Iraq scuppered a similar plan in 1992, arguing that U.N. monitoring of food distribution within Iraq violated its sovereignty.
"If it were for me to decide, I would have accepted (the offer) in 1992 but they decided not to go for it at the last minute. I blame both parties."
In May, after months of arduous negotiations, the U.N. and Iraq signed an agreement which would allow Iraq to export limited amounts of oil for the first time since the August 1990 invasion.

But in late August, just as the deal was apparently about to be implemented, Iraq got involved in fighting between two Kurdish factions in the north of the country, resulting in military retaliation by the United States.
In New York, U.N. diplomats said it could take months before the oil-for-food plan is put into practice. The United States continues to block a necessary oil pricing formula.
"The U.S. has adopted delaying tactics and it still has to approve the pricing mechanism adopted by the sanctions committee," Chalabi said.
Chalabi said there was no reason for the food distribution not to go ahead in southern Iraq, which has not been subject to the Kurdish fighting.
Chalabi said more than six years of international trade sanctions had taken its toll on the Iraqi people whose suffering may not be alleviated by the limited oil sale anyway.

Given the current high oil price, Iraq would be permitted to sell only about 500,000 barrels per day (bpd) of oil to meet the $2 billion in six months, much lower than the 700,000 bpd originally expected, he said.
"At current oil prices, Iraq would only export 500,000 bpd (but that would not be) enough to alleviate the suffering of the people. This is much below the red line," he said.
Chalabi was Iraqi oil minister between 1987 and November 1990. He was addressing the 17th Oil and Money Conference sponsored by the International Herald Tribune and the Oil Daily Co/PIW Publications.
